tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## discord-setup
Discord Server Setup MCP Server

This server provides tools for automating Discord server setup using the Discord Bot API.
It can discover servers, create/manage channels, create/manage roles, configure settings, and apply templates.

Available tool categories:
- Guild: List servers, select active server, get server info
- Channels: Create/edit/delete channels and categories
- Roles: Create/edit/delete/list/reorder roles
- Settings: Configure server verification, content filter, notifications
- Templates: Apply pre-built server templates (gaming, community, business, study-group)

Role hierarchy note: Discord positions are inverted — a HIGHER position number is
higher/more powerful, @everyone is position 0 at the bottom, and newly created
roles default to the bottom. Use list_roles to see the current order, create_role
with placement:"top"/"above"/"below" to rank a role, and reorder_roles with a
top-first orderedRoleIds list rather than hand-computing position numbers.

Prerequisites:
- Discord bot created at https://discord.com/developers/applications
- Bot token configured via DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN environment variable or ~/.discord-mcp/config.json
- Bot invited to Discord server(s) with appropriate permissions (Manage Server, Manage Roles, Manage Channels)

Setup Instructions:
1. Create a Discord application at https://discord.com/developers/applications
2. Add a bot user and copy the bot token
3. Set DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN environment variable or create ~/.discord-mcp/config.json with your token
4. Generate OAuth2 URL with bot scope and required permissions
5. Invite bot to your Discord server(s)

Workflow:
1. Use list_guilds to see available servers
2. Use select_guild to set the active server
3. Use other tools to manage channels, roles, etc.

## workos
This server manages the caller's WorkOS workspace: organizations, users, SSO connections, directories, webhooks, branding, feature flags, and more. Call list_operations once to discover operations, then run them with query (reads) or mutate (writes). whoami reports the caller's identity, role, and available environment IDs. An admin may disable mutations or this server entirely for a team; the tool response says so.

This server is a control plane for an existing workspace, not a knowledge base. For WorkOS product, integration, SDK, or tooling questions, don't guess from training data or probe package registries: read https://workos.com/docs. When integrating WorkOS into a codebase, prefer the WorkOS agent skills, which carry the deep integration guides: npx skills add workos/skills

Facts agents often guess wrong: the official WorkOS CLI is the unscoped npm package "workos" (repo github.com/workos/cli). Run npx workos@latest install for the agent-driven AuthKit installer (it edits the codebase), and use its resource commands (--json output) for scripted management. WorkOS SDKs are published under the @workos-inc npm scope (e.g. @workos-inc/node, @workos-inc/authkit-nextjs), but the CLI itself is just "workos".

content.content:
1	/**
     2	 * The decks we lay a profile out for, and the keys every profile opens with.
     3	 *
     4	 * Data only: `profiles.mjs` does the arranging. Splitting them is what lets
     5	 * the test hold a layout against a grid without running a generator, and it
     6	 * keeps the one thing a person is likely to edit - what sits where - in a
     7	 * file with no machinery in it.
     8	 */
     9	
    10	/**
    11	 * The four decks, with the numbers a layout needs.
    12	 *
    13	 * `model` is the string the Stream Deck app writes into a profile's
    14	 * `Device.Model`, taken from the app's own shipped profiles rather than
    15	 * guessed: `DefaultProfiles/StreamDeck*_winDefault.streamDeckProfile` for the
    16	 * Stream Deck, the Mini and the +, and the XL from a plugin that ships one.
    17	 * `type` is the manifest's `DeviceType`, which is the SDK's own enumeration.
    18	 *
    19	 * A + has eight keys and four dials, and they are two different controllers
    20	 * in a profile rather than twelve positions on one.
    21	 */
    22	export const DEVICES = {
    23	  xl: { model: "20GAT9901", type: 2, columns: 8, rows: 4, dials: 0 },
    24	  sd: { model: "20GAA9902", type: 0, columns: 5, rows: 3, dials: 0 },
    25	  mini: { model: "20GAI9901", type: 1, columns: 3, rows: 2, dials: 0 },
    26	  plus: { model: "20GBD9901", type: 7, columns: 4, rows: 2, dials: 4 },
    27	};
    28	
    29	/**
    30	 * The keys every profile opens with, in the order they are laid down.
    31	 *
    32	 * Connect first because nothing else does anything until it has been
    33	 * pressed, then the run it is on, then the three presses somebody reaches
    34	 * for mid-scene, then the numbers. The dedicated Roll key and the Press key
    35	 * set to the waiting roll are both here on purpose: Roll is lit only while
    36	 * dice are waiting, and Press takes the primary whatever it is, so the two
    37	 * say different things about the same moment.
    38	 *
    39	 * The clock and the dice the run throws for itself sit with the presses,
    40	 * because both are things somebody reaches for while a scene is running.
    41	 *
    42	 * The two Open keys come last but one because nothing on the deck needs
    43	 * them mid-scene: one puts the run in the browser, the other the guide.
    44	 * Finish is last of all, as far from a hand mid-scene as the layout goes,
    45	 * and it takes a hold on top of that.
    46	 *
    47	 * Fourteen keys, which is more than a Mini or a + has room for. They page.
    48	 */
    49	export const BASE = [
    50	  { action: "connect" },
    51	  { action: "run" },
    52	  { action: "next" },
    53	  { action: "roll" },
    54	  { action: "undo" },
    55	  { action: "clock" },
    56	  { action: "autoroll" },
    57	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "score" } },
    58	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "unit" } },
    59	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "clock" } },
    60	  { action: "press", settings: { target: { kind: "roll" } } },
    61	  { action: "open", settings: { target: "run" } },
    62	  { action: "open", settings: { target: "guide" } },
    63	  { action: "finish" },
    64	];
    65	
    66	/**
    67	 * What the four dials on a + carry.
    68	 *
    69	 * Only Next and Metric declare `Encoder` in the manifest, so these are the
    70	 * only two that can sit here at all. They repeat on every page of a +
    71	 * profile: paging moves the keys, and a clock you can no longer see because
    72	 * you turned to the moves is a dial doing nobody any good.
    73	 */
    74	export const DIALS = [
    75	  { action: "next" },
    76	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "score" } },
    77	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "clock" } },
    78	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "unit" } },
    79	];
    80	
    81	/**
    82	 * The packs a profile is laid out for: the demo pack, and every sketch.
    83	 *
    84	 * Paths rather than a list of packs, because the list is whatever is on
    85	 * disk. `profiles.mjs` reads the sketches folder, so a pack added to the
    86	 * repository has a profile on the next run of the generator without anybody
    87	 * editing a list here.
    88	 */
    89	export const DEMO = { slug: "demo", file: "packs/demo/pack.yaml" };
    90	export const SKETCHES = "packs/sketches";
    91	
    92	/**
    93	 * A pack's slug is its file's stem, and these are the exceptions.
    94	 *
    95	 * The slug is what names the `.streamDeckProfile` file, the manifest entry
    96	 * and the profile the plugin switches to, so changing one renames a profile
    97	 * on every deck that already has it. Elden Ring's was laid out before the
    98	 * rule existed and keeps the name it shipped under.
    99	 */
   100	export const SLUGS = { "elden-ring-tarnishedtool": "elden-ring" };

1	# Runlog for Stream Deck
     2	
     3	Runlog is a referee and run log for dice-driven games: it draws the tables, keeps the score and the clocks, and remembers what happened. This plugin puts a run on the deck's keys: the press the run is waiting on, a move, undo, and a number from the run on each key.
     4	
     5	## The keys
     6	
     7	- **Connect** opens the connection to your Runlog account, and closes it again.
     8	- **Run** names the run the deck is on; press to cycle through the runs you have open, or pick one in its settings.
     9	- **Next action** presses whatever the run is waiting on, in the step's own words.
    10	- **Press** takes one move, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer, set in the key's settings.
    11	- **Roll** throws the dice the run is waiting on.
    12	- **Keep rolling for me** hands the dice to the run so it throws them itself, and takes them back again.
    13	- **Apply setup** changes the run's loadout to a setup from your library and hands it out to the tool.
    14	- **Undo** takes back the last result.
    15	- **Metric** shows one number from the run: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps. Set to a counter or a resource it presses too: a tap steps it, a hold takes one back off.
    16	- **Clock** counts the run's clock down. Press to pause or resume it, hold to stop it.
    17	- **Finish the run** ends the run, held rather than pressed.
    18	- **Open in the browser** opens the run, its dock, a new run, the guide, or the pack's rules in your default browser.
    19	
    20	Next action, Metric and Clock also sit on a dial on a Stream Deck +.
    21	
    22	The plugin also ships laid-out profiles, one per deck for the generic keys and one per deck for every pack it bundles, built from the pack files by `npm run profiles`. The Runlog profile installs with the plugin; a pack's arrives the first time the deck follows a run of that pack, and the deck switches to it unless Connect's settings say not to.
    23	
    24	## What it needs
    25	
    26	- The Stream Deck app, 7.1 or later, on macOS 12 or Windows 10 and up.
    27	- A Runlog account, signed in from any key's settings.
    28	- A run synced to that account and open in a browser, a dock or a browser source: the deck presses through the page holding the run.
    29	- Where plans are switched on, Plus to press a run from the deck. Watching one costs nothing.
    30	
    31	## Where to read more
    32	
    33	The guide's [A Stream Deck at the table](https://runlog.scrthq.com/guide/stream-deck) sets the keys up, page by page. [Runlog](https://runlog.scrthq.com) is the app.
=== MDX ===
     1	# A Stream Deck at the table
     2	
     3	Runlog's plugin is in the Stream Deck Marketplace, under **Runlog**. Install it and twelve actions appear in the action list: Connect, Run, Next action, Press, Roll, Keep rolling for me, Apply setup, Undo, Metric, Clock, Finish the run, and Open in the browser. It needs the Stream Deck app at 7.1 or later.
     4	
     5	Profiles come with it, laid out for each deck (Stream Deck, Mini, XL and +). The Runlog profile installs with the plugin. A pack's profile has that pack's moves on keys, its counters and resources on the numbers, and its setups ready to hand out; it arrives the first time your deck follows a run of that pack, and the deck switches to it. **Switch to the pack's profile when a run attaches**, in Connect's settings, turns that off. A pack Runlog ships no profile for, one you bought or wrote yourself, puts the deck on the Runlog profile. Once a profile is yours you can rearrange it like any other.
     6	
     7	## Signing in
     8	
     9	Every key's settings carry the same account block: the Runlog address, **Sign in**, **Sign out**, **Reconnect**, and a line saying who is signed in. Leave the address alone unless you run a copy of your own.
    10	
    11	**Sign in** shows a code and a link. Open the link in a browser, type the code, and you are signed in on the deck; the plugin keeps that sign-in in a file of its own, not in the settings the pages read. Signing in is not connecting: press Connect after.
    12	
    13	## Connect
    14	
    15	The key says **Connect** while the connection is closed and **Disconnect** while it is open; press it either way. Nothing is open until you press it, and a connection holding no run closes itself after thirty minutes; the key then says _went idle_ beneath Connect. A deck that is following a run stays up however long the stream goes.
    16	
    17	Every other key says **Not connected**, with _press Connect_ beneath it, while the connection is off, and **Offline** for the moment it takes to open.
    18	
    19	## The run the deck is on
    20	
    21	The deck presses through the page that holds the run, so it only ever sees a run that is synced to your account and open on a page somewhere: the app in a browser tab, a [dock](#guide/dock), or a browser source. With nothing synced the keys say **Not synced**; with runs synced but none open, **No run open**.
    22	
    23	**Run** names the run the deck is following. Press it to cycle through the runs open to you and pin the next one; its settings list the same runs by name. A pin holds: a pinned run that ends says **That run has ended** rather than moving the deck to whichever run went next. Where one run is open and nothing is pinned, the deck follows that one; where several are open and none is pinned, the keys say **Pick a run**.
    24	
    25	## The keys
    26	
    27	- **Next action** presses whatever the run is waiting on: rolling the table, carrying on, closing the unit, entering the next. It carries the step's own words. Where the step waits on a checklist it ticks everything and presses the step's own button; where it waits on a name, it takes the first suggestion. Tick **Stop at decisions** in its settings and it leaves both to the page.
    28	- **Press** does the one thing you pick in its settings: a move the pack offers, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer.
    29	- **Roll** throws the dice the run is waiting on. It needs no settings, and is lit only while a roll is on offer.
    30	- **Keep rolling for me** hands the dice to the run so it throws them itself; press it again to take them back. The key says which of the two the run is on.
    31	- **Apply setup** changes the run's loadout to a setup from your library and hands it out to the tool, set in its settings. The list is your library for the pack's tool; a tool has to be attached to the run for the hand-out to reach it.
    32	- **Undo** takes back the last result. It is lit when there is something to take back and dim when there is not.
    33	- **Metric** shows one number and nothing else: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps. Set to a counter or a resource it is a key as well: a press steps it up by one, or puts it at a number, picked under **On press** in its settings; holding it takes one back off. The other five are the run's own arithmetic and take no press.
    34	- **Clock** counts the run's clock down on the key. Press it to pause the clock, press again to resume, and hold it to stop the clock for good. It says **No clock** where the run keeps none.
    35	- **Finish the run** ends the run, and carries the ending it would take. Hold it for a second and a half; a press says no, so the run does not end on a key caught in passing. It says **Not yet** while the run cannot end.
    36	- **Open in the browser** opens one page in your default browser, picked in its settings: the run the deck is following, that run's dock, a new run, this guide, or the pack's rules. The guide opens whether or not the deck is connected.
    37	
    38	On a Stream Deck +, Next action, Metric and Clock sit on a dial as well as a key. Turning a Metric dial steps through the score, the unit, the clock, the last result and the leader, and a running clock redraws every second. Pressing a Metric dial set to a counter or a resource steps it up by one; pressing a Clock dial pauses the clock or resumes it.
    39	
    40	A press the run has moved past, or one the page has to take, comes back refused: the key says why for three seconds, then goes back to what it was saying.
    41	
    42	## Keeping the page awake
    43	
    44	Chrome discards tabs it thinks nobody is looking at, and a discarded tab is a run the deck can no longer see. Keep the run in an OBS dock or a browser source, or exempt Runlog from Memory Saver in the browser's settings.
    45	
    46	<Note>
    47	  Where plans are switched on, pressing a run from a deck is part of Plus. Watching one (the run's name and its numbers on your keys) is
    48	  not.
    49	</Note>

    33	- **Metric** shows one number and nothing else: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps. Set to a counter or a resource it is a key as well: a press steps it up by one, or puts it at a number, picked under **On press** in its settings; holding it takes one back off. The other five are the run's own arithmetic and take no press.
    34	- **Clock** counts the run's clock down on the key. Press it to pause the clock, press again to resume, and hold it to stop the clock for good. It says **No clock** where the run keeps none.
    35	- **Finish the run** ends the run, and carries the ending it would take. Hold it for a second and a half; a press says no, so the run does not end on a key caught in passing. It says **Not yet** while the run cannot end.
    36	- **Open in the browser** opens one page in your default browser, picked in its settings: the run the deck is following, that run's dock, a new run, this guide, or the pack's rules. The guide opens whether or not the deck is connected.
    37	
    38	On a Stream Deck +, Next action, Metric and Clock sit on a dial as well as a key. Turning a Metric dial steps through the score, the unit, the clock, the last result and the leader, and a running clock redraws every second. Pressing a Metric dial set to a counter or a resource steps it up by one; pressing a Clock dial pauses the clock or resumes it.
    39	
    40	A press the run has moved past, or one the page has to take, comes back refused: the key says why for three seconds, then goes back to what it was saying.
    41	
    42	## Keeping the page awake
    43	
    44	Chrome discards tabs it thinks nobody is looking at, and a discarded tab is a run the deck can no longer see. Keep the run in an OBS dock or a browser source, or exempt Runlog from Memory Saver in the browser's settings.
    45	
    46	<Note>
    47	  Where plans are switched on, pressing a run from a deck is part of Plus. Watching one (the run's name and its numbers on your keys) is
    48	  not.
    49	</Note>

input.message:
## Summary

Reviewed the whole of `the-deck-comes-laid-out` (base `c46115d`, head `05399c7`, 9 commits, 107 files) against the plugin already on main: the profile generator and 44 shipped `.streamDeckProfile` zips, the three new actions (Open in the browser, Clock, Keep rolling for me, plus Finish the run: twelve actions total), Metric keys made pressable, the tone-per-family faces with corner glyphs and the height-aware type scale, the `Next action` rename, and the repo-wide no-em-dash guard.

Every check ran clean:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npx vitest run streamdeck apps/web/src/guide tests` | 26 files, 241 tests, all pass |
| `npm run typecheck` | exit 0 |
| `npm run lint:docs` | 0 issues in 59 files |
| `npm run format:check` | clean |
| `npm run build -w streamdeck` | built; two warnings (circular `plugin.ts` imports, TS5096) both pre-exist on `c46115d` |
| `npx streamdeck validate com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin` | Validation successful |

Additional verification I did by hand:

- **Zip container.** `Expand-Archive` of `forfeits-plus.streamDeckProfile` into `$env:TEMP` yields exactly one top-level `C0B720C8-....sdProfile/` folder, `manifest.json` with `Device: {"Model":"20GBD9901","UUID":""}` (serial empty, as required), three page folders listed in `Pages.Pages` plus a separate empty `Default`, and per page 8/8/7 keypad slots inside the 4x2 grid with 4 encoder slots. Local and central directory header field offsets are all correct, DOS date 33 is 1980-01-01, stored-only, no data descriptor.
- **Determinism and freshness.** Ran `specs()/profile()/container()` in a scratch script and compared against every committed zip: 44 of 44 byte-identical to disk, and byte-identical when built twice in the same process. `src/profiles.ts` is byte-identical to `table()`.
- **Boundaries.** The `Offer` mirror in `streamdeck/src/state.ts:17-41` matches `apps/web/src/run/offer.ts:17-35` field for field, including the `"owed"` primary id. Every press shape the plugin emits (`{ticks:"all"}`, `{subject}`, `{tracker,by}`, `{tracker,to}`, `{clock,do}`, `{autoRoll}`, `{finish:true}`) is accepted by `apps/web/src/run/takePress.ts:88-156`, and `clockPress` never sends a `do` the offer's status would refuse. `profileFor` matches all 44 manifest `Profiles` names and the 44 files on disk. `snapshot.run.packId`, which the whole switch hangs on, is real: `hosted/infra/lib/handlers/api.ts:2699-2710` returns `metricsOf(...)` with `run: {id, packId, ...}` on `GET /api/sessions/:id/snapshot`, the address `streamdeck/src/socket.ts:62` fetches.
- **Security.** Nothing secret in the profiles (pack ids, move ids, setup ids and titles, all public repo content) and nothing secret logged: `plugin.ts` logs only sign-in state and error messages, `base.ts:125` logs the face title and the key's own settings. `openUrl` only ever builds `apiBase() + <fixed path>` with `encodeURIComponent` on both the run id and the pack id, and `open.test.ts:125` pins the escaping.

Three findings, none blocking.

## Findings

### Critical

None.

### Important

**1. The "A new run" Open key says one thing and does another.**
`streamdeck/src/state.ts:364-370` vs `streamdeck/src/actions/open.ts:426-427`.

`openFace` sends every target except `guide` through `common(state)`, so a key set to `newrun` reads **Not connected** / **Not synced** / **Pick a run** and draws dim whenever the deck is not following a run. `url()` answers `newrun` before it asks anything of the run, so pressing that same dim key opens `/create` in the browser. The comment at `open.ts:426` states the intent outright ("Starting a run asks nothing of the one the deck is on, the way the guide does not"), and the two halves are separately pinned by tests that contradict each other: `state.test.ts:623` expects `openFace(open([s1, s2]), "newrun")` to be "Pick a run", while `open.test.ts:81-85` expects a press with `runs: []` to open `/create`. A streamer gets a key that looks dead and is not.

Smallest fix, matching the stated intent: in `openFace`, answer `newrun` beside `guide` before `common()` is called, for example `if (target === "guide" || target === "newrun") return { title: target === "guide" ? "Guide" : OPEN_LABELS.newrun, tone: "deck", when: "in a browser" };`, and move `state.test.ts:623` to expect "A new run". The other choice, gating `url()` on an attached run, would contradict the comment and the guide, so I would take the face change.

**2. Nothing keeps the committed zips in step with the generator.**
`streamdeck/design/profiles.test.mjs:112-116`.

The determinism test compares `container(profile(spec))` against a second in-process build, which can never catch the case that actually bites: a layout edited in `layouts.mjs`, or a move renamed in a pack YAML, committed without running `npm run profiles -w streamdeck`. The manifest listing is checked against `specs()` (line 73) and `src/profiles.ts` is checked against `table()` (line 97), so the zips are the one generated artifact with no guard. They happen to be correct today (I verified all 44), but a stale zip would ship silently and read, to whoever imported it, as the plugin being broken. The `main()` guard at `profiles.mjs:470-472` only runs when somebody runs the generator, which is exactly the case where nothing is stale.

Smallest fix: in that same test, read each `com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin/profiles/${spec.slug}-${spec.device}.streamDeckProfile` and assert `container(profile(spec)).equals(onDisk)`.

**3. Two stale comments say Clock cannot sit on a dial.**

The claim is simply no longer true.

It is worth more than a comment fix: the fourth dial on a Stream Deck + is currently `metric` set to `field: "clock"` (`layouts.mjs:78`), which is a readout that alerts on press, because `metricPress` returns null for the five fixed string fields. **6. Latent infinite loop in `paginate`.**
`streamdeck/design/profiles.mjs:158-170`: with `capacity` of 2 a continuation page computes `room = 2 - 1 - 1 = 0`, pushes an empty page, and `i += 0` never advances. `streamdeck/src/actions/base.ts:45-59`: `onWillDisappear` does not clear the action's pending `down` timestamp, so a key held while its page turns leaves an entry in the map for the life of the plugin. Bounded by the number of placements and harmless, but a `this.holds` clear on disappear would be tidy.

`streamdeck/src/state.ts:30-40` declares `setups`, `trackers`, `clock`, `autoRoll` and `ending` as required, matching the page, and then five call sites defend against an older page with `?? []` / `?? null` / `?? false` (lines 331, 434, 473, 507, 532). Per the types those guards are dead code, so a future "simplify" pass could strip them and break exactly the old-page case they exist for. ## Not tested, by design or by hardware

Called out rather than filed as findings: the hold timing feel (600 ms taps, 1500 ms on Finish), the `$B1` progress bar actually drawing from `feedback.indicator`, the inspector rows rendering under sdpi-components, and whether `switchToProfile` really installs an `AutoInstall: false` profile on first ask. ## What is good

- The generator earns its keep. Stable version-5 UUIDs off a fixed namespace, a fixed DOS timestamp and stored-only entries mean regenerating is genuinely not a diff, and the hand-written zip writer is 80 correct lines instead of a dependency. Nothing about a pack is retyped: the moves, counters, resources and setups come through the same loaders the app and CLI use, so a renamed move changes the profile rather than going quietly dead.
- `design/profiles.test.mjs` is the strongest test in the branch: it holds every key inside its own deck's grid, refuses a doubled position, allows only the twelve UUIDs plus the app's two page turns, validates each key's settings against the shape `state.ts` will read, and checks the Elden Ring profile's moves, non-hidden counters, resources and setups against the pack and the setups folder by id.

## Verdict

**Ready to open the PR.**

Findings 1 and 2 are worth fixing, but neither breaks a shipped path: finding 1 affects a key that no shipped profile places (the generic and pack profiles carry only the `run` and `guide` Open targets), and finding 2 is a guard against a mistake that has not been made, with the artifacts verified correct as committed.
